knowledge_points.label: Framing: best model under a fixed compute and data budget
knowledge_points.statement: The course's organizing question is 'what is the best model one can build given a fixed compute and data budget', i.e. accuracy = efficiency × resources, so maximize efficiency; the bitter lesson means algorithms that scale matter, not that algorithms do not matter.

anchors.quote: Right interpretation: algorithms that scale are what matter. ... accuracy = efficiency x resources ... Framing: what is the best model one can build given a certain compute and data budget?
How do you train the best model given a fixed set of resources? Today, we are compute-constrained
showed 44x algorithmic efficiency on ImageNet between 2012 and 2019

I think the wrong interpretation is that scale is all that matters. Algorithms don't matter. ... The right interpretation is that algorithms that scale are what that-- or what matters. ... efficiency is output over input, and resources is the input.
efficiency is actually, in some sense, way more important at larger scale ... if your run takes twice as long, maybe you just wait twice as long ... Even like a 5% improvement might be a big deal.
what is the best model one can build with a certain data and compute budget? ... we're going to assume that we have a lot more data than we have compute
now tomorrow, we might become data-constrained, and the calculus of what design decisions you should take might change.

provenance.filtering_note: The professor states 'accuracy = efficiency x resources' as a slogan, not a formula; the 44x ImageNet figure is cited without defining how efficiency was measured (it is the compute reduction to reach AlexNet-level accuracy in the cited paper; author inference). 'Tomorrow, we will become data-constrained' (L253) is left as a teaser. Spoken evidence (9:48): aloud the slogan gets definitions for its terms, 'efficiency is output over input, and resources is the input', so it is a little more than a slogan (the note's 'not a formula' still holds: nothing is measured). Spoken evidence (9:59-10:15): why efficiency matters more at scale, which the code states without a reason: at small scale a run that 'takes twice as long' means you 'just wait twice as long', at scale the same waste 'could be hundreds of millions of dollars', and 'Even like a 5% improvement might be a big deal'. Spoken evidence (11:09): pre-training is framed by the compute budget 'because we're going to assume that we have a lot more data than we have compute'; the data-constrained teaser (1:04:30) adds that 'the calculus of what design decisions you should take might change'.

misconceptions.belief: The bitter lesson says scale is all that matters and algorithmic work is wasted.
misconceptions.why_wrong: The professor calls that the wrong interpretation: the right one is that algorithms which scale are what matter, and efficiency matters more at larger scale because waste is unaffordable (L116-L119).

predict.q: Two teams get the same 1e25 FLOPs and the same data. Team A keeps the 2019 training recipe; team B uses one that is 4x more compute-efficient. Under the lecture's slogan accuracy = efficiency × resources, which team's result is equivalent to the other's at what multiple of compute?
predict.answer: Team B's run is equivalent to team A at 4e25 FLOPs (4x the resources).
predict.why: Efficiency multiplies resources: a 4x more efficient recipe at the same budget behaves like the old recipe with 4x the budget. That is why the course optimizes efficiency, not just scale (L118-L123).
predict.targets_misconception: The bitter lesson says scale is all that matters and algorithmic work is wasted.

transfer.q: The lecture says 'today we are compute-constrained' and lists five course topics as efficiency moves. For a lab that is instead data-constrained (plenty of GPUs, fixed small corpus), which of the lecture's five bullets (systems, tokenization, architecture, data filtering, scaling laws) changes its motivation the most, and to what?
transfer.answer: Data filtering: when compute is cheap and data is scarce, discarding data to save compute stops making sense; the goal becomes extracting more from each token (e.g. more epochs, rewriting/synthetic data) rather than 'avoid wasting compute on bad data'.
transfer.why: L250 motivates filtering by not wasting compute on bad tokens. Remove the compute constraint and that motivation inverts; the other four bullets are still about running faster on fixed hardware (L246-L251, L253).

check.q: A lab moves from being compute-constrained (the lecture's 'today') to being data-constrained: far more GPUs than it can use, and a fixed 300B-token corpus with no new data coming. Under the lecture's framing that each efficiency move exists to make the most of the scarce resource, which way should the fraction of the corpus its quality filter discards move? Answer up, down or same.
check.answer: down: the lecture motivates filtering as not wasting scarce compute on bad tokens; once compute is plentiful and tokens are scarce, throwing tokens away is the expensive move, so the filter should discard less.
check.why: L250 justifies data filtering by compute: do not spend FLOPs on low-value tokens. Swap which resource is scarce and the trade flips: discarding data now costs the scarce resource and saves the plentiful one (L246-L251, L253: 'tomorrow, we will become data-constrained').
check.varies: which resource is the binding constraint (data instead of compute), asked as a direction for one knob
check.invariant: each efficiency move is justified by the resource that is scarce; the filter's motivation follows the constraint

knowledge_points.label: Preview: training FLOPs ≈ 6·N·D
knowledge_points.statement: Training compute is approximately C = 6·N·D FLOPs for N parameters and D tokens; the lecture computes 6 × 70e9 × 1e12 = 4.2e23 FLOPs for a 70B model on 1T tokens.

anchors.quote: total_flops = 6 * 70e9 * 1e12  # Training 70B parameters on 1T tokens = 4.2e23 FLOPs @inspect total_flops
Question: given a FLOPs budget (C = 6 N D), use a bigger model (N) or train on more tokens (D)?
how many flops does training SMDB on model on 1 trillion tokens? Well, it's six times n times D roughly. And where does that come from?

provenance.filtering_note: The constant 6 is used, not derived; Lecture 2 derives it (forward 2ND + backward 4ND). The lecture does not say which FLOPs are excluded (attention over sequence length, embeddings); author inference that 6ND counts only parameter-matmul FLOPs. Spoken evidence (36:12-36:53): the formula is posed and explicitly left open ('And where does that come from?'); the answer is deferred to lecture 2 ('the basics, which we're actually going to start on next lecture', 36:12). The captions render '70B' as 'SMDB'. The 4.2e23 product is not read aloud.

prerequisites.note: 6ND is introduced as the way to state the compute budget in the framing question.

misconceptions.belief: Training FLOPs scale with parameters only; token count just changes wall-clock, not compute.
misconceptions.why_wrong: C = 6·N·D is linear in both: doubling tokens doubles FLOPs exactly as doubling parameters does (L325, L393).

predict.q: Using the lecture's formula, how many FLOPs does it take to train an 8B-parameter model on 15T tokens? Give the answer in scientific notation.
predict.why: 6 × 8e9 × 15e12 = 7.2e23. Note this is more than the 70B-on-1T example (4.2e23) even though the model is almost 9x smaller: D enters linearly (L325).
predict.targets_misconception: Training FLOPs scale with parameters only; token count just changes wall-clock, not compute.

transfer.q: You have a fixed budget of 4.2e23 FLOPs (the lecture's example). You decide to halve the parameter count from 70B to 35B. By the 6ND rule, how many tokens can you now train on?
transfer.why: D = C / (6N) = 4.2e23 / (6 × 35e9) = 2e12 tokens. Halving N doubles the affordable D at fixed C (L393).

retrieval.q: Write the lecture's one-line estimate for training FLOPs in terms of N parameters and D tokens.
retrieval.answer: C ≈ 6·N·D

retrieval.q: The lecture's worked number: a 70B model on 1T tokens costs how many FLOPs?

prompts.self_explain: Why does a formula with only N and D, and no sequence length, work as a first estimate of Transformer training compute?

presentations.notice: C is linear in N and in D alike: an 8B model on 15T tokens costs more than the lecture's 70B model on 1T.

knowledge_points.label: Compute-optimal rule of thumb: D ≈ 20·N
knowledge_points.statement: Classic compute-optimal scaling (Chinchilla) says roughly D = 20·N tokens per parameter, so a 70B model should see about 1.4T tokens; this ignores inference cost, which pushes toward smaller models trained longer.

anchors.quote: TL;DR: D = 20 N is roughly optimal (e.g., 70B parameter model should be trained on ~1.4T tokens) ... Caveat: this doesn't take into account inference costs (want a smaller model)
Classic compute-optimal scaling laws
how should you balance training a larger model versus training on more tokens? ... the classic compute optimal scaling laws from Kaplan et Al and the so-called Chinchilla scaling laws comes in.

for each FLOPs budget, so let's say 6e18 all the way to 3e21, you sweep across different model sizes and you choose the best one. ... if you're unlucky, it's going to be all over the place, which means that you should have no confidence

this is quite crude, but a rule of thumb is, the 20 times the number of parameters is the number of data points you should train on. ... depending on the data set and architecture, this number will actually vary. ... A lot of models these days are small, but they're trained on way more tokens than is compute optimal

provenance.filtering_note: The lecture states the 20:1 ratio as a TL;DR without the ISOFLOP fitting that produces it (shown only as a figure, L395-L397); the full derivation is deferred to the scaling-laws lectures and Assignment 3 (L405-L411). PaLM is described as 'undertrained' (L150), which is this rule applied in hindsight. Spoken evidence (49:43-50:27): the ISOFLOP procedure is narrated, not only shown: for each budget (6e18 to 3e21, read off the figure) sweep model sizes, keep the best, fit a curve; if the optima do not fall on a line 'you should have no confidence' in the extrapolation. Correction to this note: 'without the ISOFLOP fitting that produces it (shown only as a figure)' is too strong; the code has the two ISOFLOP bullets (L395-L396) and the professor walks through them aloud; what is missing is the fitting arithmetic. Spoken evidence (50:27-51:09): the rule is called 'quite crude' and said to vary with dataset and architecture, and the inference caveat is explained: 'A lot of models these days are small, but they're trained on way more tokens than is compute optimal' because a smaller model is cheaper to serve.

prerequisites.note: The question 'bigger N or more D' is posed in terms of C = 6ND.

misconceptions.belief: Given more compute, the best move is always a bigger model.
misconceptions.why_wrong: Compute-optimal scaling grows N and D together (D ≈ 20N); a model trained on far fewer than 20 tokens per parameter is undertrained, which is the lecture's description of PaLM (L150, L398).

predict.q: You are handed a budget of 1e25 FLOPs and follow the lecture's rule D = 20·N with C = 6·N·D. Roughly how many parameters should the model have? Give billions.
predict.why: C = 6·N·(20N) = 120·N², so N = sqrt(1e25 / 120) ≈ 2.9e11 ≈ 290B parameters, trained on D ≈ 5.8T tokens.
predict.targets_misconception: Given more compute, the best move is always a bigger model.

transfer.q: Same 1e25 FLOPs, but the lecture's caveat applies: the model will serve billions of queries, so you deliberately choose a 70B model instead of the compute-optimal size. How many tokens does the budget buy, and how does that compare to the 20·N rule?
transfer.answer: D = 1e25 / (6 × 70e9) ≈ 2.4e13 ≈ 24T tokens, about 340 tokens per parameter, far above 20·N. The model is 'overtrained' on purpose to be cheaper at inference.
transfer.why: Fixing N below optimal at fixed C pushes all remaining compute into D. The lecture's caveat (L399) is exactly that inference cost makes this trade worthwhile.

check.q: A team has a budget of 6e23 FLOPs and, for inference cost, fixes the model at N = 10B parameters instead of the compute-optimal size. Using C = 6·N·D, how many training tokens per parameter (D / N) does the budget buy? Type only the number.
check.why: D = C / (6N) = 6e23 / (6 × 1e10) = 1e13 tokens; D / N = 1e13 / 1e10 = 1000, fifty times the 20·N rule. Fixing N below the compute-optimal size at fixed C pushes all the remaining compute into tokens, which is the lecture's inference-cost caveat (L393-L399).
check.targets_misconception: Given more compute, the best move is always a bigger model.
check.varies: the budget and the fixed model size; asks tokens per parameter rather than total tokens
check.invariant: at fixed C = 6ND, choosing N determines D; a smaller-than-optimal N means many more tokens per parameter than 20

retrieval.answer: About 1.4T (D = 20·N)

retrieval.answer: Inference cost; including it favors a smaller model (trained on more tokens) (L399).

knowledge_points.label: Why tokenization is an efficiency decision
knowledge_points.statement: Tokenization matters for compute because it sets sequence length: attention is quadratic in sequence length, so compressing 1000 bytes into ~250 tokens cuts context cost, and raw bytes are 'elegant but compute-inefficient' with today's architectures.

anchors.quote: Efficiency lens - Reduce context length (1000 bytes → ~250 tokens) - Adaptive computation (more modeling capacity on interesting parts of input)
Tokenization: working with raw bytes is elegant, but compute-inefficient with today's model architectures
the sequences will be too long. Given that the context length of a Transformer is limited (since attention is quadratic), this is not looking great...
The dream: tokenizer-free model architectures, which operate directly on bytes ... These are promising, but have not yet been scaled up to the frontier.

through an efficiency lens, tokenization is good because it takes a long sequence ... reduces it into a smaller number of tokens. But more subtly, but maybe more importantly, it allows you to do adaptive computation. ... some of the more rare or interesting parts of input should be left as multiple tokens.
the dream is to really have an end-to-end way that directly operates on bytes. ... so far, these have not been scaled to the frontier. And since the frontier models are still using tokenizers
Tokenization, as I mentioned before, you can't just work with raw bytes, but that's going to be very compute inefficient, at least with today's model architectures.
chunks should be variable. You want adaptive computation. Not all bytes are treated the same.

provenance.filtering_note: The professor says 'attention is quadratic' without separating attention FLOPs from the (linear-in-length) matmul FLOPs that dominate at short context; a 4x longer sequence costs 4x in the MLP/projection terms and 16x only in the score computation (author inference, see Lecture 2). The 'adaptive computation' bullet is asserted, not demonstrated. Tokenizer-free models (ByT5, MegaByte, BLT, H-Net) are cited as a dream, not taught. Spoken evidence (28:55-29:15): adaptive computation is ranked above sequence shortening ('more subtly, but maybe more importantly') and explained: a stretch of many bytes can become one token while 'rare or interesting parts of input should be left as multiple tokens', so the model spends more positions, and so more compute, on them. The code's bullet only names it. The reason for still teaching tokenizers is said aloud: 'since the frontier models are still using tokenizers' (29:42).

misconceptions.belief: Tokenization is a preprocessing detail with no effect on training cost.
misconceptions.why_wrong: Token count per byte sets sequence length, and attention cost grows with the square of sequence length; a 4x worse compression ratio means 4x more tokens for the same text (L276, L610, L673).

predict.q: A document is 1000 bytes. Tokenizer A yields 250 tokens (the lecture's figure); tokenizer B is byte-level. If attention cost were purely quadratic in sequence length, by what factor is attention more expensive under B than under A?
predict.why: B gives 1000 tokens vs 250: 4x the length, so (4)² = 16x the attention-score cost. The linear terms (projections, MLP) would be only 4x more (L276, L673).
predict.targets_misconception: Tokenization is a preprocessing detail with no effect on training cost.

transfer.q: A tokenizer-free byte model (the lecture's 'dream') is proposed for a corpus of 8 KB-average documents, previously handled at ~4 bytes per token so that one document fills a 2048-token context. If nothing else changes, what context length in tokens would it need to see whole documents, and which lecture claim explains why that is a problem today?
transfer.answer: About 8192 bytes-as-tokens (4x longer); the problem is that Transformer context is limited because attention is quadratic, so 'raw bytes are elegant but compute-inefficient with today's architectures' (L248, L673).
transfer.why: Bytes per token drops from ~4 to 1, multiplying sequence length by 4; the lecture frames byte-level models as not yet scaled to the frontier for exactly this cost reason (L279-L280).

check.q: A tokenizer averaging 3 bytes per token is replaced by one averaging 4.8 bytes per token on the same documents. Treating attention cost as purely quadratic in sequence length, the new attention cost for a document is what fraction of the old one? Give a decimal; type only the number.
check.why: Sequence length scales as bytes / (bytes per token), so it falls by 3 / 4.8 = 0.625. Quadratic attention cost falls by 0.625² ≈ 0.39. This is the lecture's reason tokenization is an efficiency decision: compression sets sequence length and attention is quadratic in it (L275-L277, L248).
check.targets_misconception: Tokenization is a preprocessing detail with no effect on training cost.
check.varies: direction (better compression instead of none) and the bytes-per-token values
check.invariant: sequence length is inversely proportional to bytes per token, and attention cost is quadratic in sequence length

retrieval.answer: 1000 bytes → ~250 tokens (L276).

retrieval.q: Name the two benefits the lecture's 'efficiency lens' lists for tokenization.
retrieval.answer: Reduce context length; adaptive computation (more capacity on interesting parts of the input) (L276-L277).

retrieval.answer: Compute-inefficient with today's architectures, because sequences become too long for quadratic attention (L248, L673).

knowledge_points.label: Tokenizer = encode/decode between strings and integer indices
knowledge_points.statement: A tokenizer is a pair of functions, encode: str → list[int] and decode: list[int] → str, and a language model places a probability distribution over the resulting integer sequences; a correct tokenizer round-trips (decode(encode(s)) == s).

anchors.quote: class Tokenizer(ABC): ... def encode(self, string: str) -> list[int] ... def decode(self, indices: list[int]) -> str

A language model places a probability distribution over sequences of tokens (usually represented by integer indices). ... So we need a procedure that *encodes* strings into tokens. We also need a procedure that *decodes* tokens back into strings.
Check that encode() and decode() roundtrip: ... assert string == reconstructed_string
formally, a tokenizer converts between raw inputs, which are just bytes, and a sequence of integers, which represent the tokens. Conceptually, it's a segmentation of the text.

raw text is what is text? It's Unicode strings. ... the language model places a distribution over sequences of tokens usually represented as indices. ... a tokenizer is basically something that can do this round trip.
tokenizers should round trip. If you implement tokenizer, it doesn't round trip, you have a problem.

provenance.filtering_note: The lecture asserts the round-trip on one string per tokenizer; it never shows a tokenizer that fails to round-trip (e.g. decoding an index sequence that splits a multi-byte UTF-8 character). Special tokens are deferred to Assignment 1 (L724).

misconceptions.belief: The model sees text; tokenization is just how text is stored.
misconceptions.why_wrong: The model's distribution is over integer index sequences (L583-L584); it never sees characters, so two tokenizers give the model two different problems for the same text.

predict.q: The lecture's example `indices = [15496, 11, 995, 0]` is the GPT-2 encoding of 'Hello, world!'. If you decode those same four integers with the GPT-5 (o200k) tokenizer, what do you expect to get, and why?
predict.answer: Some unrelated string (or garbage), not 'Hello, world!': indices only mean something relative to the vocabulary of the tokenizer that produced them.
predict.why: encode and decode are a matched pair over one vocab (L256-L262). The GPT-5 tokenizer encodes the lecture's 'Hello, 🌍! 你好!' as [13225, 11, 130321, 235, 0, 220, 177519, 0], completely different ids for 'Hello' (13225 vs 15496).
predict.targets_misconception: The model sees text; tokenization is just how text is stored.

transfer.q: You write a tokenizer whose encode lowercases the input before mapping to indices. Which of the lecture's two required procedures breaks, and which lecture check would catch it?
transfer.answer: decode cannot recover the original casing, so the round-trip assert `string == reconstructed_string` (L606) fails on any input with uppercase letters.
transfer.why: The interface demands decode(encode(s)) == s; any lossy encode violates it even if the model trains fine (L603-L606).

check.q: Which of these encode designs keeps the lecture's round-trip check decode(encode(s)) == s true for every Unicode string?
choices: replace every non-ASCII character with one shared id
collapse each run of spaces into a single space id
emit one id per UTF-8 byte of each character
map each word to the id of its lowercase form
check.answer: emit one id per UTF-8 byte of each character
distractor_from: 'one shared id for non-ASCII' <- misconception: 'The model sees text; tokenization is just how text is stored.' (treats a lossy mapping as a harmless storage detail)
'collapse runs of spaces' <- same misconception: whitespace looks like formatting, but it is part of the string
'lowercase form' <- the transfer's own failure (lossy casing), here as a distractor
check.why: Only the byte mapping is invertible: every string has a unique UTF-8 byte sequence and decode can concatenate and decode it. The other three map distinct strings to the same ids, so decode cannot recover which one it was and the assert at L606 fails (L603-L606).
check.targets_misconception: The model sees text; tokenization is just how text is stored.
check.varies: the learner picks the lossless encode among several instead of diagnosing one lossy encode
check.invariant: a tokenizer must be invertible on every input: decode(encode(s)) == s

retrieval.q: Give the two method signatures of the lecture's abstract Tokenizer class.
retrieval.answer: encode(string: str) -> list[int]; decode(indices: list[int]) -> str (L258-L262).

retrieval.q: What single assertion does the lecture run on every tokenizer it builds?
retrieval.answer: assert string == reconstructed_string (decode(encode(s)) == s).

knowledge_points.label: What a production BPE tokenizer looks like (space-prefixed tokens, digits)
knowledge_points.statement: In GPT-style tokenizers, a word and its preceding space form one token (' world'), the same word at the start vs the middle of a string gets different ids, and numbers are split every few digits.

anchors.quote: A word and its preceding space are part of the same token (e.g., " world"). A word at the beginning and in the middle are represented differently (e.g., "hello hello"). Numbers are tokenized into every few digits.
tokenizer = get_gpt5_tokenizer() ... indices = tokenizer.encode(string)  # @inspect indices
play with this interactive site

you'll appreciate why tokenizers are kind of annoying and why people want to get rid of them. ... many tokens you'll actually see are space a word ... this hello and this hello is actually two completely different indices that have nothing to do with each other.

numbers are represented with-- every few digits is a token. Sometimes, it's predictable, and sometimes, it's not. Some tokenizers try to make every digit a token, but then you're blowing up the number of tokens you have.

provenance.filtering_note: The three observations are stated for the learner to verify on the interactive site; the lecture does not explain their cause (the GPT-2 pre-tokenization regex attaches a leading space to each word and caps digit runs), which is deferred to Assignment 1 (L725). The GPT-5 trace value for 'Hello, 🌍! 你好!' is [13225, 11, 130321, 235, 0, 220, 177519, 0]: 8 tokens, where the emoji costs two tokens (130321, 235). Spoken evidence (1:06:47-1:06:57): the digit rule is given a trade-off the code lacks: digit chunking is 'sometimes predictable, sometimes not', and one-token-per-digit is the alternative, at the price of 'blowing up the number of tokens'. The first observation is garbled aloud ('a word conglomerate with its preceding space are different tokens', 1:06:14) but the next sentence agrees with L594-L595. The interactive site did not load in class (1:05:56), so the observations were stated, not demonstrated.

misconceptions.belief: A tokenizer maps each word to one id, independent of where it appears.
misconceptions.why_wrong: The leading space is part of the token, so 'hello' at the start and ' hello' after a space are two different ids (L595-L596).

predict.q: Encode the string 'hello hello' with a GPT-style tokenizer. How many distinct token ids do you expect, and what explains the count?
predict.answer: Two distinct ids: 'hello' and ' hello' (space attached to the second occurrence).
predict.why: The space before a word is part of its token, so the first and second 'hello' differ (L595-L596).
predict.targets_misconception: A tokenizer maps each word to one id, independent of where it appears.

transfer.q: You fine-tune a model on prompts that always end with a trailing space before the answer ('Answer: '). At inference you send 'Answer:' with no trailing space. Using the lecture's observations, what changes in the token stream the model sees?
transfer.answer: During training the answer word was tokenized without its leading space (the space was consumed by the prompt); at inference the answer word now absorbs the space and becomes a different token (' word' vs 'word'), so the model sees ids it rarely saw after 'Answer:'.
transfer.why: Space attachment makes token identity depend on the character before the word (L595).

check.q: A GPT-style tokenizer encodes 'red red' as the ids [a, b]. Using the lecture's observation about spaces, what does it produce for 'red red red'?
distractor_from: '[a, a, a]' <- misconception: 'A tokenizer maps each word to one id, independent of where it appears.'
'[a, b, a]' <- plausible: treats the id as alternating with position rather than depending on the preceding character
'[a, b, c]' <- plausible: treats every occurrence as a new token
check.why: The first 'red' has no preceding space (id a); every later one is ' red' with the space attached (id b). Token identity depends on the character before the word (L594-L597).
check.targets_misconception: A tokenizer maps each word to one id, independent of where it appears.
check.varies: a repeated-word encoding instead of a prompt-boundary scenario
check.invariant: the preceding space is absorbed into the word's token, so position after a space changes the id

retrieval.q: In the lecture's example ' world', which character is part of the token that a naive word splitter would drop?
retrieval.answer: The leading space.

knowledge_points.label: Vocabulary size trades sequence length against sparsity
knowledge_points.statement: Raising vocabulary size raises compression ratio (shorter sequences) but makes rare tokens sparse; GPT-5's vocab is 200,019, versus 256 for bytes and a lower bound of 127,758 for Unicode code points.

anchors.quote: One could increase compression ratio by increasing **vocabulary size** (number of possible token values increases), leading to sparsity. ... vocabulary_size = tokenizer.n_vocab  # @inspect vocabulary_size

Problem 1: this is a very large vocabulary. Problem 2: many characters are quite rare (e.g., 🌍), which is inefficient use of the vocabulary. ... worst of both worlds (large vocabulary, low compression ratio)
The vocabulary is nice and small: a byte can represent 256 values. ... The compression ratio is terrible, which means the sequences will be too long.

you could obviously increase the compression ratio by increasing the vocab size, but then, you get into sparsity where more and more-- because every element of vocab is treated like a distinct element. So these days, tokenizers, especially multilingual tokenizers, have 100k or 200k tokens

provenance.filtering_note: 'Sparsity' is left undefined; author inference: each token id's embedding and output row is updated only when that id occurs, so a huge vocab of rare ids learns slowly and costs parameters (see supp-vocab-embedding-params). The lecture never states a recommended vocab size; it shows the trade-off by example (256 → ratio 1.0; 200,019 → ratio 2.5). Spoken evidence (1:07:56-1:08:22), correcting two claims in this note: 'sparsity' gets a partial gloss aloud, 'because every element of vocab is treated like a distinct element', which is the start of the author's reading above (each id is learned on its own); and although no size is recommended, a typical range is given: 'these days, tokenizers, especially multilingual tokenizers, have 100k or 200k tokens'. The vocabulary file is skipped 'in the interest of time' (1:08:25).

misconceptions.belief: A bigger vocabulary is strictly better because every token carries more text.
misconceptions.why_wrong: The character tokenizer has a huge vocabulary (≥127,758) and still a poor ratio (1.538), and most of its ids are rare: large vocab alone buys nothing unless the entries are frequent (L643-L648).

predict.targets_misconception: A bigger vocabulary is strictly better because every token carries more text.

transfer.q: A team doubles their BPE vocabulary from 50K to 100K and observes the average compression ratio rise from 4.0 to 4.3. Using the lecture's trade-off, name one cost that rose and estimate how much shorter the sequences became.
transfer.answer: Sequences are about 7% shorter (4.0/4.3 ≈ 0.93x tokens). Costs: sparsity, since the 50K new ids are the rarest merges and get few gradient updates, and (inference) twice the embedding/output rows.
transfer.why: Compression gains from extra vocab are diminishing because new merges are increasingly rare; the sparsity cost is linear in the added ids (L611).

check.q: Growing a BPE vocabulary from 32K to 64K raises the average compression ratio from 3.6 to 4.0 bytes per token. On a fixed corpus, the new token count is what fraction of the old one? Give a decimal; type only the number.
check.why: Tokens = bytes / ratio, so the token count scales by 3.6 / 4.0 = 0.9: sequences are 10% shorter for twice the vocabulary, while 32K new, rare ids must each be learned (L611-L612).
check.targets_misconception: A bigger vocabulary is strictly better because every token carries more text.
check.varies: vocabulary sizes and ratios; asks the sequence-length side of the trade only
check.invariant: token count is inversely proportional to compression ratio; added vocabulary gives diminishing length savings

retrieval.q: What single lever does the lecture name for increasing compression ratio, and what downside does it attach?
retrieval.answer: Increase vocabulary size; leads to sparsity (L611).

assert ord("a") == 97 ... assert ord("🌍") == 127757 ... assert chr(127757) == "🌍"

There are approximately 150K Unicode characters. ... vocabulary_size = max(indices) + 1  # This is a lower bound @inspect vocabulary_size ... Problem 1: this is a very large vocabulary. ... This tokenizer is the worst of both worlds (large vocabulary, low compression ratio).
Unicode string, that's a sequence of Unicode characters. And each character is an integer, which you can call ord in Python ... there are 150k Unicode characters.
your vocab size could be 150k, which is a lot. I mean, it's not crazy, but I think the bigger problem is that many characters are actually rare ... So this is not a very good tokenizer.

provenance.filtering_note: The '150K Unicode characters' figure is cited from Wikipedia (L643) and the code reports only a lower bound from the example string (max code point + 1). The lecture does not mention that code points go up to 0x10FFFF (1,114,112), so a true 'all code points' vocab is larger than 150K assigned characters. GPT-5's 200k vocabulary is larger, so size alone cannot be the objection.

misconceptions.belief: A character tokenizer has compression ratio exactly 1 since one character is one token.
misconceptions.why_wrong: The ratio counts UTF-8 bytes per token, and non-ASCII characters are multi-byte; the lecture's string gives 20 bytes / 13 tokens = 1.538 (L647).

knowledge_points.label: UTF-8 is variable length: 1 to 4 bytes per character
knowledge_points.statement: UTF-8 encodes each Unicode code point as 1 to 4 bytes, each in 0..255: 'a' is one byte, '你' is three (e4 bd a0), '🌍' is four (f0 9f 8c 8d), so 'Hello, 🌍! 你好!' is 13 characters but 20 bytes.

string = "Hello, 🌍! 你好!"  # @inspect string ... indices = tokenizer.encode(string)  # @inspect indices
The most common Unicode encoding is UTF-8
Unicode has a UTF-8 encoding, which means that you can-- sometimes a string like "a" is just 1 byte, and sometimes, a string is multiple bytes.

provenance.filtering_note: The lecture shows 1-byte and 4-byte examples only; the 2- and 3-byte cases (é, CJK) and the rule that trailing bytes always lie in 0x80-0xBF are not taught. That the CJK characters in the example take 3 bytes each is read from the trace (indices 228,189,160 and 229,165,189), not stated in prose.

knowledge_points.label: Byte tokenizer: vocab 256, compression ratio exactly 1
knowledge_points.statement: A byte tokenizer encodes a string as its UTF-8 bytes (integers 0..255), giving a tiny fixed vocabulary of 256 but a compression ratio of exactly 1.0 for every input, so sequences are as long as the text's byte length.

anchors.quote: class ByteTokenizer(Tokenizer): ... string_bytes = string.encode("utf-8") ... indices = list(map(int, string_bytes))

vocabulary_size = 256 ... compression_ratio = get_compression_ratio(string, indices) ... assert compression_ratio == 1 ... The compression ratio is terrible, which means the sequences will be too long.

notice that this is a longer sequence now, but all the numbers are between 0 and 255 ... And the compression ratio is 1, which is not great. So byte sequences can be very long, but the vocab size is small.

provenance.filtering_note: The lecture asserts ratio == 1 on one string; that it is identically 1 for all strings follows from the definition (bytes / bytes) and is left for the learner to notice. The lecture does not discuss that decode can fail on an index sequence that is not valid UTF-8 (author inference).

misconceptions.belief: The byte tokenizer's compression ratio depends on the text (e.g. it is worse for emoji-heavy text).
misconceptions.why_wrong: Ratio = bytes / tokens and each byte is one token, so it is exactly 1.0 for any string; the text only changes the sequence length, not the ratio (L670-L671).

predict.q: The byte tokenizer gives ratio 1.0 on 'Hello, 🌍! 你好!'. What ratio does it give on a 5,000-character Chinese document?
predict.why: Every UTF-8 byte becomes exactly one token, so bytes / tokens = 1 regardless of script. The document would be ~15,000 tokens long, but the ratio is still 1 (L670-L671).
predict.targets_misconception: The byte tokenizer's compression ratio depends on the text (e.g. it is worse for emoji-heavy text).

transfer.why: Byte tokens are not characters; a language model emitting byte ids can produce sequences no character maps to, which a character-level tokenizer could not (L522-L523, L658).

check.q: '你' is the three UTF-8 bytes [228, 189, 160]. Which index list makes the lecture's ByteTokenizer.decode raise a UnicodeDecodeError?

'[0, 127]' <- plausible: edge values look invalid, but both are single-byte ASCII code points
check.why: decode calls bytes(indices).decode('utf-8') (L521-L524). [228, 189] opens a three-byte sequence that is never completed, so it is not valid UTF-8. Byte ids are not characters, so a byte-level model can emit sequences no string maps to.

check.invariant: a byte sequence decodes only if every multi-byte UTF-8 sequence in it is complete

knowledge_points.label: Word tokenizer: good compression, unbounded vocabulary, UNK
knowledge_points.statement: Splitting with the regex \w+|. gives meaningful word tokens and a high compression ratio (5.5 on the lecture's example) but a vocabulary that is the set of distinct chunks in the training data: unbounded, full of rare words, and forcing an UNK token for unseen words.

anchors.quote: string = "I'll say supercalifragilisticexpialidocious!" ... chunks = regex.findall(r"\w+|.", string)  # @inspect chunks
vocabulary_size = "Number of distinct chunks in the training data" ... compression_ratio = get_compression_ratio(string, chunks) ... Compression ratio is good, but vocabulary size can be huge.

Many words are rare and the model won't learn much about them. This doesn't obviously provide a fixed vocabulary size. New words we haven't seen during training get a special UNK token, which is ugly and can mess up perplexity calculations.

this is what actually people used to do in NLP ... each token is meaningful because humans invented words, and words tend to have a stable semantic meaning. But your vocab size is the number of distinct chunks in the training data

the vocabulary could be actually unbounded, right? Because at test time, you might get some sequence and you tokenize, and then you have a token you've never seen before. ... UNK token, but that's really ugly and can mess up your perplexity calculations.

provenance.filtering_note: The chunks are ['I', "'", 'll', ' ', 'say', ' ', 'supercalifragilisticexpialidocious', '!']: 8 chunks over 44 bytes = 5.5. The lecture never actually builds the chunk→int mapping (vocabulary_size is a string). How UNK 'messes up perplexity' (the model can get easy credit for predicting UNK) is asserted, not shown. Spoken evidence (1:11:32-1:11:47): why 'no fixed vocabulary size' (L694) bites: the training set fixes the vocabulary, but at test time 'you have a token you've never seen before', which is what forces UNK. The appeal of words is also given: 'words tend to have a stable semantic meaning' (1:11:09).

misconceptions.belief: Word tokenization fails mainly because words are too long to be useful tokens.
misconceptions.why_wrong: Long tokens are the good part (ratio 5.5). It fails because the vocabulary is unbounded and open-ended: rare words are learned poorly and unseen words collapse to UNK (L690-L695).

predict.q: Apply the lecture's regex \w+|. to "I'll say supercalifragilisticexpialidocious!" (44 bytes). How many chunks result, and what is the compression ratio?
predict.why: \w+ grabs runs of alphanumerics (I, ll, say, supercali...), and '.' grabs each remaining single character (', two spaces, !) as its own chunk (L680, L689).
predict.targets_misconception: Word tokenization fails mainly because words are too long to be useful tokens.

transfer.q: A word tokenizer is trained on English news, then evaluated on a chemistry corpus full of names like 'tetrahydrocannabinol'. Which of the lecture's three 'moreover' problems bites first, and what happens to the token stream?
transfer.answer: The UNK problem: unseen words map to a single UNK id, so most chemical names become identical UNK tokens and the text (and the perplexity) loses information.
transfer.why: Vocabulary is 'the number of distinct chunks in the training data'; anything outside it has no id (L688, L695). BPE avoids this because its base vocab (bytes) covers everything.

check.q: A word tokenizer uses the lecture's regex \w+|. (so each space and the period is its own chunk), and its vocabulary is every distinct chunk of the training text 'the cat sat on the mat.'. It then encodes 'the dog sat on the rug.'. How many of the output ids are UNK? Type only the number.
check.why: Training chunks: 'the', ' ', 'cat', 'sat', 'on', 'mat', '.'. In the test sentence 'dog' and 'rug' are not in that set, so both become UNK; every other chunk, including the spaces and the period, is known (L688-L695).
check.varies: a tiny explicit vocabulary instead of a domain shift, so the count can be traced
check.invariant: the vocabulary is exactly the set of training chunks; any other chunk has no id and maps to UNK

retrieval.q: What is the vocabulary size of the lecture's word tokenizer, in the lecture's own words?
retrieval.answer: The number of distinct chunks in the training data (L688).

retrieval.q: Name the three problems the lecture lists under 'Moreover' for word tokenization.
retrieval.answer: Many words are rare so the model learns little about them; no fixed vocabulary size; unseen words become an UNK token that messes up perplexity (L693-L695).

knowledge_points.label: BPE: a data-driven vocabulary of frequent byte sequences
knowledge_points.statement: Byte Pair Encoding (Gage 1994 for compression; Sennrich et al. 2016 for NMT; used by GPT-2) trains a tokenizer on raw text: start with each byte as a token and repeatedly merge the most common adjacent pair, so common byte sequences become single tokens and rare ones stay as many tokens.

anchors.quote: The BPE algorithm was introduced by Philip Gage in 1994 for data compression. ... It was adapted to NLP for neural machine translation. ... BPE was then used by GPT-2.

Basic idea: *train* the tokenizer on raw text to construct a vocabulary tailored to the data. Intuition: common sequences of bytes are represented by a single token, rare sequences are represented by many tokens. Sketch: start with each byte as a token, and successively merge the most common pair of adjacent tokens.
This unit was inspired by Andrej Karpathy's video on tokenization

byte pair encoding. And this was introduced a long time ago for data compression. ... It was first introduced to NLP for doing neural machine translation. And the first paper that used BPE for LLMs was GPT-2.

train the tokenizer on raw text to construct a vocabulary that's tailored to the data. ... If it's rare, then it just breaks up into smaller units rather than having this UNK token. ... Rare sequences are going to be split into multiple tokens.

provenance.filtering_note: Sennrich's original BPE merged characters within words (word-level pre-tokenization); the byte-level variant with a 256-byte base vocab is GPT-2's contribution. The lecture collapses the two. 'Most common' is a greedy choice; the lecture does not claim optimality for compression (summary: 'an effective heuristic', L497). Spoken evidence (1:12:36-1:12:46): BPE is tied explicitly to the word tokenizer's failure: everything 'can be tokenized', because a rare string 'just breaks up into smaller units rather than having this UNK token'. The code's intuition line (L706) gives the common/rare split but not the no-UNK consequence.

prerequisites.note: BPE's base vocabulary is the byte tokenizer's 256 values.
BPE is presented as the fix for the word tokenizer's unbounded vocabulary.

misconceptions.belief: BPE is a fixed algorithmic mapping like UTF-8: the same string always gives the same tokens regardless of training data.
misconceptions.why_wrong: BPE is trained; its merges depend on which pairs were frequent in the training corpus, so two BPE tokenizers trained on different text tokenize the same string differently (L705-L706).

predict.q: Two BPE tokenizers with the same vocab size are trained, one on English Wikipedia and one on Python source code. Which gives the higher compression ratio on a Python file, and which lecture sentence predicts this?
predict.answer: The code-trained one; 'train the tokenizer on raw text to construct a vocabulary tailored to the data' / 'common sequences of bytes are represented by a single token'.
predict.why: Merges are chosen by frequency in the training corpus, so sequences common in code (e.g. 'def ', '    ') become single tokens only if the training text contained them often (L705-L706).
predict.targets_misconception: BPE is a fixed algorithmic mapping like UTF-8: the same string always gives the same tokens regardless of training data.

transfer.q: A string contains a byte sequence that never appeared in BPE training. Contrast what the word tokenizer and the byte-level BPE tokenizer each produce for it.
transfer.answer: The word tokenizer emits an UNK id; byte-level BPE falls back to the individual bytes (ids 0..255), so the text is still represented exactly, just with many tokens.
